def: Delivery of a strong electric shock across the chest to depolarize the whole heart at once, letting the sinus node regain control. Used for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia.
An exaggerated fall in systolic blood pressure (more than 10 mmHg) during inspiration. Classic for cardiac tamponade; also seen in severe asthma or COPD exacerbations.
The stage of fetal lung development (about weeks 16 to 26) when bronchioles enlarge and become vascularized and type II pneumocytes first appear. Gas exchange becomes possible near its end.
Merging together into one continuous area instead of staying as separate spots or nodules, as in confluent lobar consolidation or a confluent rash.
A sudden flare-up or worsening of a chronic disease, such as an acute asthma or COPD attack.
Violet-purple in color, describing skin lesions such as the plaques of lupus pernio or the rash of dermatomyositis.
A rare inherited bleeding disorder caused by defective platelet GPIb, so platelets cannot bind von Willebrand factor. Gives a low platelet count with abnormally large platelets.

Thin, protein-poor fluid that leaks into a body space because of pressure or oncotic imbalance, as in heart failure, cirrhosis or hypoalbuminemia. Contrasts with protein-rich exudate from inflammation.
Acid excreted in urine bound to buffers, mainly phosphate (H2PO4-). It is measured by titrating urine back to pH 7.4 with base.
Flattening or thinning out of a normally raised structure. In the kidney, podocyte foot processes flatten in nephrotic syndromes such as minimal change disease; in labor, the cervix thins.
Absence or loss of spleen function, from surgical removal or autosplenectomy in sickle cell disease. Leaves patients prone to overwhelming infection by encapsulated bacteria.
Spinal muscular atrophy type 1, a severe autosomal recessive loss of anterior horn motor neurons from SMN1 deletion. Causes a floppy infant with symmetric weakness and tongue fasciculations.
Relating to the ear, particularly the external ear (auricle or pinna), as in auricular pain or the auricular branch of a nerve.
Tiny aneurysms on small penetrating brain arteries (e.g., lenticulostriates), caused by chronic hypertension. Rupture causes intracerebral hemorrhage in the basal ganglia, thalamus or pons.
Made of a disorganized overgrowth of tissue types native to the site. Hamartomatous polyps occur in Peutz-Jeghers and juvenile polyposis.
Constriction of a bowel loop or other tissue that cuts off its blood supply, leading to ischemia and infarction, as in an incarcerated hernia or volvulus.
A small opening in the sphenoid bone of the skull base that carries the middle meningeal artery into the cranial cavity.
Relating to a spinal nerve root. Radicular pain shoots along the nerve's dermatome, as in sciatica from a herniated disc.
Gram-positive cocci that grow in grape-like clusters and are catalase positive. Includes Staphylococcus aureus (coagulase positive) and S. epidermidis.
A small, solid, raised skin bump less than 1 cm across, as in lichen planus or acne.
A break of the distal humerus just above the elbow, common in children after falling on an outstretched hand. Can injure the brachial artery, risking Volkmann contracture.
A bony bump above a joint's condyle at the end of the humerus or femur. The medial and lateral humeral epicondyles anchor the forearm flexors and extensors (golfer's and tennis elbow).
Passing across the placenta from mother to fetus, as with ToRCH infections or IgG antibodies.
Untwisting of a torsed organ, such as an ovary, to restore its blood supply (also called detorsion).
Passage of an infection from mother to child before, during or soon after birth, including breastfeeding.
Round bacteria that occur in pairs. Examples are Neisseria species (gram-negative) and Streptococcus pneumoniae (gram-positive).
A liver enzyme that attaches glucuronic acid to bilirubin and many drugs to make them water soluble. Deficiency causes Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar syndromes and gray baby syndrome in preterm infants.
A syndrome of tremor, rigidity and slowed movement resembling Parkinson disease. Can be drug-induced, especially by dopamine D2 blockers such as antipsychotics.
Back-and-forth, non-propulsive contractions of the intestine that mix contents with secretions and speed absorption, unlike forward-moving peristalsis.
An abnormally high neutrophil count in the blood, seen with bacterial infection, glucocorticoids or stress.
Round, concentrically layered calcified deposits seen under the microscope. Classic for papillary thyroid carcinoma, also meningioma, serous ovarian cancer and mesothelioma.
One of the two main ketone bodies, made in the liver from fat breakdown during fasting or diabetic ketoacidosis. Detected by the urine nitroprusside test.
One of a pair of erectile tissue columns in the penis (and the clitoris) that fill with blood to cause erection.
Smooth flow in parallel layers with little mixing, occurring at a low Reynolds number. It is quiet, whereas turbulent flow makes murmurs and bruits.
Describing a swelling that moves like fluid under the examiner's fingers when pressed, typical of an abscess with pus.
Chaotic, swirling flow at a high Reynolds number (fast flow, large vessel, low viscosity). It creates audible murmurs and bruits.
How easily an ion crosses a membrane through open channels. High resting K+ conductance keeps the resting potential near the K+ equilibrium potential.
The early phase of ventricular systole after the mitral valve closes and before the aortic valve opens. Pressure rises while volume stays constant because all valves are closed.
A narrow band joining two larger parts. The aortic isthmus lies just beyond the left subclavian artery and is the usual site of coarctation and traumatic rupture.
A stain that turns iron-containing deposits blue. Used to show hemosiderin in tissue and ringed sideroblasts in bone marrow.
A neck muscle running from the mastoid process to the sternum and clavicle that turns and tilts the head. Supplied by the accessory nerve and used as an accessory muscle of inspiration.
A flat, dull thud on tapping the chest, instead of normal resonance, indicating solid or fluid beneath, such as pneumonia consolidation or pleural effusion.
Excess air trapped in the lungs, flattening the diaphragm and widening the intercostal spaces. Typical of COPD and asthma attacks.
The embryonic tissue (blastema) that the ureteric bud induces to become nephrons, from the glomerulus through the distal tubule.
Producing no echoes on ultrasound, so it appears black. Typical of fluid-filled simple cysts.
Relating to the diencephalon, the forebrain region containing the thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus and subthalamus.
Small cavities or spaces. In bone each lacuna houses an osteocyte, and empty lacunae signal osteonecrosis; cartilage lacunae hold chondrocytes.
Tiny blue dots in red cells on a blood smear, from clumped ribosomal RNA. Seen in lead poisoning, thalassemia and sideroblastic anemia.
Deformation of red cells into rigid crescents when deoxygenated hemoglobin S polymerizes in sickle cell disease. Causes vaso-occlusion and hemolysis.
A brainstem nucleus in the lower medulla that relays fine touch, vibration and proprioception from the lower body, via the fasciculus gracilis of the dorsal column.
Spinal muscular atrophy type 1, a severe autosomal recessive loss of anterior horn motor neurons from SMN1 deletion. Causes a floppy infant with symmetric weakness and tongue fasciculations.
Above the clavicle. An enlarged left supraclavicular node (Virchow node) can signal abdominal cancer such as gastric carcinoma.
Death of tissue with decay and dark discoloration after loss of blood supply or severe infection.
A rare autosomal recessive disorder of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase causing unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and jaundice. Type I is severe with kernicterus; type II responds to phenobarbital.
An X-linked recessive immunodeficiency from a WAS gene mutation, causing eczema, recurrent infections and thrombocytopenia with small platelets.
An X-linked recessive immunodeficiency from a WAS gene mutation, causing eczema, recurrent infections and thrombocytopenia with small platelets.
Abnormally hardened or dense. Sclerotic (osteoblastic) bone lesions appear white on radiographs, as in prostate metastases.
Skin that shears off when rubbed or stroked, because the epidermis separates from deeper layers. Positive in pemphigus vulgaris, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Dissolving a blood clot with drugs such as alteplase, used in acute ischemic stroke, massive pulmonary embolism and myocardial infarction.
Protrusion of abdominal organs through a wound or surgical incision.
Small hand muscles that flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints. The lateral two are supplied by the median nerve, the medial two by the ulnar nerve.
Thin partitions dividing a structure into compartments. Septate fungal hyphae (e.g., Aspergillus) have cross-walls, unlike Mucor, and cysts may contain septations.
An organism that grows without oxygen. Obligate anaerobes such as Actinomyces, Bacteroides and Clostridium are killed by oxygen; aminoglycosides are ineffective against them.
A gram-negative bacterium that causes granuloma inguinale (donovanosis), a sexually transmitted painless genital ulcer with a beefy red base and Donovan bodies.
Following a dermatome, the strip of skin supplied by one spinal nerve root, as in shingles from varicella-zoster reactivation.
A family of enveloped, negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses with fusion proteins that cause cells to merge into syncytia. Includes measles, mumps, RSV and parainfluenza.
Overuse injury in adolescent athletes causing painful inflammation of the tibial tuberosity where the patellar tendon attaches, from repeated quadriceps traction.
The neurotoxin of Clostridium tetani that travels up motor neurons and cleaves SNARE proteins, blocking inhibitory neurotransmitter release. Causes spastic paralysis (lockjaw).
Short hairlike protein appendages on bacteria that attach them to host surfaces. Fimbria variation in Neisseria gonorrhoeae prevents effective vaccination.
A single-celled eukaryotic organism, some of which are parasites. Examples are Plasmodium, Giardia, Entamoeba, Toxoplasma and Trypanosoma.
